back: The knowledge, skills and behaviors needed to guide, motivate and direct a team to help the organization achieve its goals.
Management directs using positional power. Leadership guides and influences using relational power.
Management: systems, control, near-term goals, how and when. Leadership: relationships, trust, long-range vision, what and why.
Leading by understanding and addressing the needs and development of team members, to enable the highest team performance.

front: Centralized vs distributed management and leadership
back: Centralized: top-down, authority with top management. Distributed: authority spread among individuals and teams; teams may self-organize.
The ability to identify, assess and manage your own emotions and those of other people and groups.
Self-awareness, self-management, social awareness, social skills.
Realistic self-assessment: understanding your own emotions, goals, motivations, strengths and weaknesses.
Also called self-regulation: controlling and redirecting disruptive feelings and impulses; thinking before acting.
Empathy: understanding and considering other people's feelings, reading non-verbal cues, active listening.
Managing groups, building rapport and networks, finding common ground. The culmination of the other three EI areas.
Scarce resources, scheduling priorities, personal work styles.
Collaborate/problem-solve, compromise/reconcile, smooth/accommodate, force/direct, withdraw/avoid.
Combine viewpoints through open dialogue to reach consensus and commitment. Win-win.
Each party gets some satisfaction; a partial or temporary resolution. Can be lose-lose.
Emphasize agreement over difference; concede to maintain harmony and relationships.
Push one viewpoint at the expense of others, usually from a power position, to resolve an emergency. Win-lose.
Retreat from the conflict or postpone it, to be better prepared or to let others resolve it.
Early, usually in private, with a direct, collaborative approach. Team members first; the project manager facilitates if it escalates.

front: Four values of the PMI Code of Ethics
back: Responsibility, respect, fairness, honesty.

front: Who does the Code of Ethics apply to?
back: PMI members, certification holders, applicants in a certification process, and PMI volunteers.
Aspirational: conduct we strive to uphold. Mandatory: firm requirements; violations go to PMI's Ethics Review Committee.
Our duty to take ownership for the decisions and actions we take or fail to take, and their consequences.
Our duty to show a high regard for ourselves, others and the resources entrusted to us.
Our duty to make decisions and act impartially and objectively, free from self-interest, prejudice and favoritism.
Our duty to understand the truth and act truthfully in our communications and conduct.

front: Conflict of interest: what must you do?
back: Disclose it fully and proactively, and stay out of the decision until there is a mitigation plan and stakeholder consent. Even the appearance counts.

front: When may an ethics complaint be filed?
back: Only when it is substantiated by facts. Retaliating against someone who raised a good-faith concern is itself a violation.
No. Half-truths, information out of context and withholding information that makes a statement misleading all violate the honesty standards.
Open communication, shared understanding, shared ownership, trust, collaboration, adaptability, resilience, empowerment, recognition.
Five steps an individual goes through in a change: Awareness, Desire, Knowledge, Ability, Reinforcement.
Top-down: create urgency; form a powerful coalition; create a vision; communicate the vision; remove obstacles; create short-term wins; build on the change; anchor it in the culture.
Late status quo; the foreign element; chaos (lowest performance); the transforming idea; practice and integration; new status quo.
Change is situational, transition is psychological. Stages: ending, losing and letting go; the neutral zone; the new beginning.
Formulate change; plan change; implement change; manage transition; sustain change.
By competence and commitment, the style moves from directing to coaching to supporting to delegating.
Outcome, Situation, Choices / consequences, Actions, Review.
Orientation (why), trust building (who), goal clarification (what), commitment (how), implementation, high performance, renewal.

front: Six ways of addressing conflict (7th edition)
back: Confronting / problem solving; collaborating; compromising; smoothing / accommodating; forcing; withdrawal / avoiding.
Outcomes of a negotiation: win-win (best), win-lose or lose-win, lose-lose. Win-win needs character, trust and approach.
